Sample Size for AIPE on a Pearson Correlation

Source: R/ss_aipe_r.R
ss_aipe_r.Rd

Determines the sample size needed for a confidence interval on a population Pearson correlation \(\rho\) to have a desired width (accuracy in parameter estimation; Kelley & Maxwell, 2003). The interval planned for is the Fisher's Z interval that correlations_test reports for method = "pearson": the correlation is transformed as \(Z(r) = \mathrm{atanh}(r)\), an interval with standard error \(1/\sqrt{N - 3}\) is formed on the Z scale, and the limits are back-transformed through \(\tanh(\cdot)\) (Fisher, 1921; Bonett & Wright, 2000, Equation 2). Because the plan targets the same interval the analysis will report, the planned width and the analyzed width agree.

Usage

ss_aipe_r(true_cor, width, conf_level = 0.95, assurance = NULL)

Arguments

true_cor

Population Pearson correlation \(\rho\) the sample size is planned for, in \((-1, 1)\). The planner treats this value as the truth; ss_aipe_r_sensitivity shows what the plan delivers when the truth (true_cor there) differs from the value planned with (supposed_cor there).

width

Desired full width of the confidence interval on the correlation.

conf_level

Desired confidence level (default 0.95). A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused (see "Small tail areas" in ci_nc_t).

assurance

Optional. The probability that the realized interval is no wider than width. The function returns the smallest sample size, at or above the sample size planned without it, at which that probability is at least assurance. A single number above 0.5 and below 1; when NULL (the default) the plan is for the width at \(r = \rho\) only.

Value

A data.frame with the columns term and value and one row per term:

necessary_N

the planned total sample size.

expected_width

the full width of the interval at necessary_N when the sample correlation equals true_cor.

true_cor, width, conf_level

the inputs.

assurance

the requested probability; present only when assurance was given.

assurance_attained

the probability, at necessary_N and true_cor, that the realized interval is no wider than width; present only when assurance was given. It is at least assurance, and above it because the sample size is a whole number or because the plan without assurance already exceeds the request.

Details

Closed-form first pass. On the Fisher's Z scale the interval has half-width \(z_{1 - \alpha/2} / \sqrt{N - 3}\), and the delta method maps it back to the correlation scale as approximately $$w \;\approx\; 2\, z_{1 - \alpha/2} \, \frac{1 - \rho^2}{\sqrt{N - 3}},$$ which solves to the first-stage approximation of Bonett and Wright (2000), $$n_0 \;=\; 3 + \Big\lceil 4\, (z_{1 - \alpha/2})^2 (1 - \rho^2)^2 / w^2 \Big\rceil.$$ Here and below \(\rho\) is true_cor, \(w\) is width, and \(1 - \alpha\) is conf_level.

Exact iteration. The back-transformed width depends on \(\rho\) through \(\tanh(\cdot)\), so the delta method approximation can land a few observations off in either direction. Starting from \(n_0\), the function evaluates the exact back-transformed width \(\tanh(z_\rho + z_{1 - \alpha/2}/\sqrt{N - 3}) - \tanh(z_\rho - z_{1 - \alpha/2}/\sqrt{N - 3})\) and steps the integer \(N\) until it is the smallest sample size whose width is at or below width. Where Bonett and Wright (2000) stop after a single second-stage adjustment, this search is exact.

The assurance step. A plan without assurance makes the interval as narrow as the target when the sample correlation equals true_cor; in many samples it is wider. With assurance the function finds the sample size at which the realized interval is no wider than the target with at least that probability, from the sampling distribution of the sample correlation r of N independent observations from a bivariate normal population:

  1. At a given N the width of the interval depends on the sample only through r, and it decreases as \(|r|\) grows. The realized interval is therefore no wider than the target exactly when \(|r| \ge r^*(N)\), where \(r^*(N)\) is the root of \(\tanh(\mathrm{atanh}(r) + z_{1 - \alpha/2}/\sqrt{N - 3}) - \tanh(\mathrm{atanh}(r) - z_{1 - \alpha/2}/\sqrt{N - 3}) = w\). When the width at \(r = 0\), the widest the interval can be, already meets the target, every sample does and the probability is 1.

  2. The distribution function of r is computed as $$F(c) \;=\; \int_0^1 T_{2N - 3}\!\Big(\sqrt{2N - 3}\, \Big\{\frac{c\,\sqrt{1 - b}}{\sqrt{1 - c^2}} - \frac{\rho\,\sqrt{b}}{\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}}\Big\}\Big)\, g(b)\, db,$$ where \(T_{2N - 3}\) is the distribution function of Student's t on \(2N - 3\) degrees of freedom and \(g\) is the density of the beta distribution with parameters \((N - 1)/2\) and \((N - 2)/2\). The form follows from writing \(r / \sqrt{1 - r^2}\) as \((Z + \theta \sqrt{U}) / \sqrt{V}\), with \(Z\) standard normal, \(U\) and \(V\) chi square on \(N - 1\) and \(N - 2\) degrees of freedom, all independent, and \(\theta = \rho / \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\), and then conditioning on \(U / (U + V)\). It is the computation ss_aipe_partial_r uses with no variables partialed out.

  3. The probability at N is \(P_N = 1 - F(r^*(N)) + F(-r^*(N))\), and the function returns the smallest N, at or above the sample size planned without assurance, with \(P_N \ge\) assurance, found by doubling a step upward and then bisecting. assurance_attained is \(P_N\) at that N.

The probability is exact, up to numerical integration, under bivariate normality. It was checked against the density of r computed from its hypergeometric series, and against the proportion of intervals no wider than the target among samples of bivariate normal data. The search does not go below the plan without assurance, so a plan with assurance is never smaller than the plan without it. Near \(\rho = 0\) a slightly smaller N can attain the probability, because there the interval at \(r = 0\) is barely wider than the target (at \(\rho = 0\) and a width of .10 the probability is .917 at 1537, one below the plan without assurance). At and above the plan without assurance, \(P_N\) did not decrease from one N to the next in any of the 15 planning sets scanned (\(|\rho|\) of 0, .1, .5, .9, and .99 with widths of .05, .1, and .2). The result depends on true_cor only through \(|\rho|\). At true_cor = 0 the plan without assurance already makes every interval as narrow as the target, since the interval is widest at \(r = 0\); assurance then adds nothing and assurance_attained is 1. As \(|\rho|\) grows the width becomes more variable from sample to sample and the step adds more: for a width of .10 and an assurance of .80 the plan moves from 62 to 83 at \(\rho = .90\).

Why the step is not a chi square factor. Multiplying the sample size planned without assurance by \(\chi^2_{\gamma, N - 2} / (N - 2)\), the \(\gamma\) quantile of a chi square on \(N - 2\) degrees of freedom over its degrees of freedom, with \(\gamma\) the assurance, does not serve here. That factor is the \(\gamma\) quantile of the ratio of a sample variance to its population value, so it applies to an interval whose width is proportional to a sample standard deviation; the width of the interval for a correlation depends on the sample through r instead. At true_cor = .90, a width of .10, and an assurance of .80 the factor gives 72, where the probability is .672 (83 are needed); with an assurance of .99 it gives 92, where the probability is .887 (122 are needed). At true_cor = 0 it gives more than the plan without assurance, which already attains a probability of 1.

The planning value matters least near zero. At a fixed sample size the back-transformed width is largest at \(\rho = 0\) and shrinks as \(|\rho|\) grows, so a planning value closer to zero yields a larger, more conservative sample size. When little is known about the population correlation, true_cor = 0 gives the sample size that suffices for any population value.

When to use simple vs. partial correlation planning. Use this function when the inferential target is the correlation between two variables with nothing partialed out. When the target is the correlation after statistically controlling for other variables, see ss_aipe_partial_r.

The Monte Carlo companion ss_aipe_r_sensitivity evaluates how the plan behaves when the population correlation differs from the planning value.

References

Bonett, D. G., & Wright, T. A. (2000). Sample size requirements for estimating Pearson, Kendall and Spearman correlations. Psychometrika, 65(1), 23–28. doi:10.1007/BF02294183

Fisher, R. A. (1921). On the "probable error" of a coefficient of correlation deduced from a small sample. Metron, 1, 3–32.

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 9 on correlations.)

Examples

# Plan N so the 95% CI on the Pearson correlation has full width
# at most 0.20, when the anticipated correlation is 0.30.
ss_aipe_r(true_cor = 0.30, width = 0.20)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    320  
#>  expected_width 0.200
#>  true_cor       0.300
#>  width          0.200
#>  conf_level     0.950
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# A narrower target width requires a larger sample size.
ss_aipe_r(true_cor = 0.30, width = 0.10)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    1274 
#>  expected_width 0.100
#>  true_cor       0.300
#>  width          0.100
#>  conf_level     0.950
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The smallest N at which the realized interval is no wider than
# 0.20 with probability at least .80. The last row is the probability
# at the returned N.
ss_aipe_r(true_cor = 0.30, width = 0.20, assurance = 0.80)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        336  
#>  expected_width     0.195
#>  true_cor           0.300
#>  width              0.200
#>  conf_level         0.950
#>  assurance          0.800
#>  assurance_attained 0.805
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# At a large correlation the width varies more from sample to sample,
# and the assurance step adds more cases.
ss_aipe_r(true_cor = 0.90, width = 0.10)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    62   
#>  expected_width 0.100
#>  true_cor       0.900
#>  width          0.100
#>  conf_level     0.950
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
ss_aipe_r(true_cor = 0.90, width = 0.10, assurance = 0.80)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        83   
#>  expected_width     0.085
#>  true_cor           0.900
#>  width              0.100
#>  conf_level         0.950
#>  assurance          0.800
#>  assurance_attained 0.807
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Planning at true_cor = 0 gives the sample size that suffices for any
# population correlation, since the interval is widest there.
ss_aipe_r(true_cor = 0, width = 0.20)
#>  term           value
#>  necessary_N    385  
#>  expected_width 0.200
#>  true_cor       0    
#>  width          0.200
#>  conf_level     0.950
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
